questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of data-driven testing?
options: Tests run faster than any other style
One test logic is reused across many input/expected-output rows, so adding a case means adding data, not code
It removes the need for assertions
It makes tests independent of the application
questions.explanation: Separating logic from data avoids copy-pasted tests. It does not make tests faster per case or remove assertions.

questions.prompt: Each data row should include the expected result, not just the input.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Without the expected value the test can only check that nothing crashed. Pairing input with expected outcome is what makes each row a real test.

questions.prompt: In JUnit 5, which source supplies comma-separated rows inline in the annotation?
options: @ValueSource
@CsvSource
@MethodSource
@EnumSource
questions.explanation: @CsvSource takes rows like "2, 3, 5". @ValueSource gives one value per invocation, @MethodSource calls a factory method, @EnumSource iterates enum constants.

questions.prompt: How many times does this test run?
questions.explanation: @CsvSource has three rows, so the method runs three times; each row is split on commas into the two parameters.

questions.prompt: A data file has a row `discount=10%` and the test fails with NumberFormatException. What is the most robust fix?
options: Wrap the test in try/catch
Store values in the format the test expects (10) or parse explicitly in one helper, and validate the data file before tests run
Delete the row
Use a String for every parameter and never convert
questions.explanation: Bad test data should fail fast with a clear message, and conversion belongs in one place. Swallowing exceptions or deleting the case hides problems.

questions.prompt: Which data sources are reasonable for data-driven tests? Select all that apply.
options: Inline annotations for a handful of small cases
CSV or JSON files in the test resources folder for larger tables
Production database tables queried live during the test
A factory method that builds rows in code
questions.explanation: Inline, file-based and factory-built data are all versioned with the tests. Live production data is unstable, can contain personal data and makes results unreproducible.

questions.prompt: Why give each parameterised case a readable name (for example JUnit's `name = "{0} -> {1}"`)?
options: It makes tests faster
So a failure in the report says which row failed without opening the data file
It is required for CSV sources
It enables parallel execution
questions.explanation: Readable display names turn 'validatesEmail[2] failed' into 'ana@ -> false failed', which speeds up triage.

questions.prompt: A form has 4 fields with 5 meaningful values each. Testing all combinations needs 625 rows. What is a sound way to cut this down?
options: Pick 10 random rows
Use pairwise (all-pairs) combinations plus specific rows for known high-risk combinations
Test only the first value of each field
Run all 625 through the UI every commit
questions.explanation: Pairwise covers every pair of values in far fewer rows, which catches most interaction bugs, and adding risk-based rows covers what matters most. Random sampling has no coverage guarantee; first-value only misses nearly everything.

questions.prompt: Your data-driven login test runs 50 rows through the UI and takes 12 minutes. Most rows check password rules. What change gives the biggest win?
options: Run with a faster machine
Move the password-rule rows to unit or API tests and keep 2-3 UI rows that prove the wiring
Add Thread.sleep to stabilise it
Split it into 50 separate test classes
questions.explanation: Validation rules are logic; testing them below the UI is faster and more precise. The UI only needs to show the rules are connected. Splitting classes or bigger machines keep the wrong-level problem.

coding.title: Check pairwise coverage
coding.prompt:
Write `uncovered_pairs(params, rows)`.

- `params` maps parameter name to list of values, e.g. `{'browser': ['chrome','firefox'], 'os': ['win','mac']}`.
- `rows` is a list of dicts, each giving one value per parameter.

Return a sorted list of every value pair not covered by any row, as tuples `(name1, value1, name2, value2)` where `name1 < name2` alphabetically.

```python
uncovered_pairs({'a':[1,2],'b':['x','y']}, [{'a':1,'b':'x'}])
# [('a',1,'b','y'), ('a',2,'b','x'), ('a',2,'b','y')]
```
coding.explanation: Every pair of parameters (combinations) and every pair of their values (product) must appear in at least one row for full pairwise coverage. Sorting the names first guarantees name1 < name2. This checker is how you verify that a reduced pairwise table really covers all pairs.
hints: itertools.combinations(sorted(params), 2) gives each parameter pair once.
itertools.product gives all value pairs for those two parameters.
A pair is covered if any(row[n1] == v1 and row[n2] == v2 for row in rows).
